Chapter 2: Social Currency—Why People Share What Makes Them Look Good
Let’s dive into why we love sharing things that make us look good. It all comes down to something called social currency. That’s the value we get from sharing stories, tips, or discoveries that help us stand out. Think of it like a kind of social money—we use it to buy attention, approval, and status from the people around us.
Picture this: you stumble across a hidden speakeasy tucked away in your city. You’re one of the first to know, and telling your friends about it doesn’t just help them—it tells everyone you’re adventurous, in-the-know, and maybe even a bit cooler than the rest.
That feeling of being ahead of the curve? It’s what drives a lot of what we share with others.
Social currency shows up in a few different ways. Let’s break them down.
First up, remarkability. People love talking about things that are surprising, new, or just plain impressive. The more remarkable something is, the more likely you’ll want to tell someone about it. Maybe it’s a product with a wild feature you’ve never seen before, a story with a jaw-dropping twist, or a service that just blows away your expectations. When something delights or surprises you, it’s almost impossible not to share.
Next, there’s insider knowledge. Being in on a secret or having access to exclusive info makes us feel special. And when we share that with others, we get to show off a little—like we’re part of an exclusive club. That’s why things like secret menus, limited-time offers, or members-only events get people buzzing. They make us feel unique, and they give us something cool to tell our friends.
Then we have game mechanics. Competition, achievements, or even just a little status boost can really drive sharing. Think about the apps that reward you with badges or points, or those loyalty programs at your favorite coffee shop. When people earn something, they want others to see it. Sharing those badges or showing off a high score isn’t just about the achievement—it’s about the recognition you get from other people.
Here’s a fun example: imagine a fast-food chain launches a secret menu item. Only people who know about it can order it. If you’re one of them, you feel like an insider—and chances are, you’ll tell your friends. Pretty soon, word spreads. The restaurant gets more customers talking, all without spending a dime on extra advertising.
Social currency goes way beyond just products or services. It’s everywhere—in the articles we share to look smart, the jokes we pass on to seem witty, or the causes we support to show our values. Underneath it all, there’s the same motivation: we want to look good in the eyes of others.
So, how can you tap into this? It starts with designing things that people actually want to talk about. That means focusing on what makes something truly remarkable, giving people a taste of exclusivity, or building in ways for them to show off their achievements. And don’t forget to make sharing easy—whether it’s through social media, word of mouth, or even just a quick text.
If you want to build social currency into your ideas or products, try these practical steps:
Create features or experiences that surprise people or give them a great story. Offer exclusive access or insider info. And add some friendly competition or ways to recognize achievements.
At the end of the day, when people feel that sharing something will make them look good, you’d better believe they’ll spread the word. And that’s how you make your ideas and products truly contagious.
